title: Practical Poisoning Attacks with Limited Byzantine Clients in Clustered Federated Learning
abstract: The presence of non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data among clients poses a critical challenge to the deployment of Federated Learning (FL) in practice. In response, state-of-the-art solutions known as Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) schemes, such as FL+HC and PACFL, have emerged to tackle this issue. Their main innovation is to cluster non-IID clients into groups of IID clients, such that techniques designated for IID scenarios can be easily applicable. Nonetheless, the robustness of CFL schemes remains largely unexplored, and existing Byzantinerobust defence mechanisms prove inadequate in CFL schemes and non-IID data settings. In this work, we present novel powerful CFL-specific poisoning attacks, named Cluster-U-M and Cluster-U-D. These attacks are designed to significantly reduce the model utility, measured in terms of test accuracy, for benign clients participating in the CFL schemes. Notably, these attacks remain agnostic, requiring no adversarial knowledge regarding defense solutions and benign clients themselves. At a high level, the attacks involve two steps, including cluster poisoning attacks and client-drift exploitation within clusters. The former induces the grouping of clients with different training distributions, and the latter amplifies the difference between each client's optimum and their group's average aggregation. We extensively evaluate the impact of these attacks using FL+HC and PACFL schemes on both small and large scales. The evaluation results demonstrate that the attacks can compromise up to 54% of clients, with a maximum accuracy loss of 48%. Even with only 0.1% clients compromised, which represents a minimal practical adversarial effort, these attacks can still victimize around 4% clients. We evaluate the effectiveness of two stateof-the-art Byzantine-robust defence mechanisms, i.e., FLTrust and FLAME, in countering Cluster-U-M and Cluster-U-D, and find that the attacks can victimize up to 38% of clients with an accuracy loss of 18-38% under the FL+HC scheme.

Introduction Federated Learning (FL) enables multiple clients to col- laboratively train a global model without sharing their pri- vate data [32]. However, a practical challenge in the FL de- ∗Corresponding author. ployment is the statistical data heterogeneity among clients, known as non-independent and identically distributed (non- IID) data [20], [24], [25], [30], [42], [44]. For instance, nearby clinics may capture unique diseases in distinct ge- ographical areas, but these clinics still wish to participate in an FL-based healthcare system. Empirical studies [26], [28] have shown that FL suffers from significant accuracy loss, ranging from 20% to 55% on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, and can even result in random guessing for face recognition [23] due to the non-IID nature. Recently, clustered Federated Learning (CFL) schemes, such as FL+HC [9], PACFL [43] FMTL [37], and IFCA [21], have gained wide attention for addressing the non-IID data challenge. The key component in a CFL scheme is a clustering solution that identifies clients with similar local updates (e.g., FL+HC) or training datasets (e.g., PACFL), thereby enabling more effective optimization of the local empirical loss for clients within the same cluster. Experi- mentally, PACFL and FL+HC demonstrate an up to 2.1× ac- curacy improvement compared to FedAvg [32]. Compared with weight generalization approaches, i.e., Scaffold [26], FedProx [42], and FedNova [45], PACFL also improves the accuracy 23% − 55% [43]. As promising, CFL schemes have been widely adopted in real-world applications of recommendation [34], [46], [50], graph learning [11], [48], edge networking [29], video processing [27], multi-model learning [21], and IoThealthcare [52]. Despite the wide adoption of CFL schemes, their ro- bustness has not been thoroughly investigated. Sattler et. al [38] is the only study of this kind, with a focus on FMTL scheme [37]. However, FMTL assumes a fixed number of client groups, which is impractical as shown in FL+HC [9] and PACFL [43]. Additionally, Sattler et al. [38] do not account for benign clients belonging to different groups to study non-IIDness. From defense perspective, state-of-the- art FL defenses, such as FLTrust [10], FLAME [33], and DeepSight [36], have not rigorously evaluated with CFL schemes and non-IID data settings. For instance, the label distribution skew setting [23], [28], where the distribution of labels varies across clients. In this study, we investigate the robustness of CFL schemes through the lens of novel practical poisoning at- tacks under non-IID data settings. Specifically, we introduce two untargeted poisoning attacks called Cluster-U-M 1751 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00163 and Cluster-U-D attacks, incorporating a practical attack model. The goal of these attacks is to degrade the prediction accuracy of benign FL clients on any random classes. The attacker only has access to compromised clients and views the server using a CFL scheme as a black box. A real-world example of these attacks is a mobile user who possesses a non-IID training dataset consisting of her preferred news categories (labels), such as sports and fashion news [21]. However, after participating in FL using a CFL scheme, the user's model starts misclassifying sports and fashion articles, confusing them with other categories, like political articles and criminal news. To accomplish this attack goal, we design a two-step approach for the attacks. During the first step, our key insight is that a clustering operation is introduced in CFL schemes to resolve the non- IID data challenge, forming groups of IID clients. Hence, our attack goal is to poison the clustering process to alter the clustering structure. This alteration results in parts of the clusters being split into smaller clusters while others are merged to form larger ones. As a result, the attacks can reintroduce the presence of non-IID clients (along with compromised clients) within the same clusters, disrupting the usage of FedAvg in optimizing the loss. In the second phase, we design the attacker to con- tinuously poison the local updates (or the training data) of compromised clients in individual clusters. In that way, our attacks aim to cause a drift in the updates of each client, slowing down their learning convergence (aka. client- drift effect). As a result, the poisoned updates render the aggregated model of the cluster unstable and slow to con- verge, since clients in the same clusters are learning with different optimizing directions. Remarkably, we have proven and shown that our attacks even succeed in clusters of purely benign clients without compromised clients. In this manner, minimal efforts from the attackers (with only 0.1% compro- mised clients) are adequate to make the attacks successful. We evaluated our attacks on FL+HC and PACFL schemes. Our evaluation investigates attack capability , at- tack practicality, and defense effectiveness. Considering the FL attack practicality raised in a recent study [40], we specifically focused on practical scenarios where compro- mised client proportion is less than 20%. The client sizes evaluated also range from small-scale ( 50 − 102 clients) to large-scale (1 × 103 − 2 × 103 clients). Both are to give less favor to the proposed attacks, compared with the evaluation in existing attacks [3], [8], [12], [18], [39], to reveal the extent of their practicality. Yet, we systematically adapt the widely used label skew setting in [23], [28], [32], [43] to simulate the non-IID phenomenon practically. On attack capability, we found that Cluster-U-M and Cluster-U-D attacks victimize up to 54% of the clients, resulting in an absolute accuracy loss at maximum 48% when the server clusters clients based on their local updates (i.e., the FL+HC scheme). Numerically, above 500 clients out of 1×103 benign ones become victims under the attacks. In PACFL, the Cluster-U-M attacks can victimize up to 60% of the clients with a loss up to 50%. We then evaluated the proposed attacks with even lower proportions of compromised clients ( 0.1% − 1%), as She- jwalka et al. [40] emphasized that poisoning attacks become a significant concern when 0.1% of benign clients are compromised, due to the practical cost and effort of the at- tacker. Our evaluation shows that even with a compromised proportion as low as 0.1% − 1%, Cluster-U-M attacks can victimize 3.2% − 4.3% of clients with an accuracy loss of 10% − 30% when the FL+HC scheme is in use. Intuitively, one compromised client is enough to make 32 victim clients out of 1 × 103 benign clients losing 30% prediction accuracy. This loss is reduced to 11%−17% with respect to Cluster-U-D attacks. On defense effectiveness , we evaluated the proposed attacks against the state-of-the-art solutions FLTrust [10] and FLAME [33]. FLTrust normalizes the impact of poi- soned local updates using a trusted bootstrapping dataset, and FLAME clusters and adaptively clips malicious updates. We found that FLTrust and FLAME indeed do not capture the clustering step. As a result, the attacker can still bypass the defense and poison the clustering step in the FL+HC scheme, further exploiting the client-drift effect within clus- ters of benign clients. In our experiment, we demonstrated that even with FLTrust deployed, the attacker can still victimize [1% − 11%] of benign clients with an absolute accuracy loss of [20% − 30%]. For instance, 50 compro- mised clients is enough to make 152 clients out of 1 × 103 benign ones losing 20% accuracy. Similarly, with FLAME, the attacks impact [1.5% − 38%] of benign clients with [18% − 20%] loss. Contributions. Our contributions are summarized as fol- lows. • We present the first study investigating the robust- ness of CFL schemes. Specifically, we formalize new cluster poisoning attacks (§4.2) and the exploitation of client-drift effect in CFL schemes (§4.3). • We introduce Cluster-U-M and Cluster-U-D attacks, and analyse them with CFL schemes (§4.4). • We extensively evaluate the attacks in practical FL settings, considering compromised proportions and client scales, even when state-of-the-art defenses FLTrust [10] and FLAME [33] are employed (§5). • We discuss new defense solutions with experimental evaluation and shed light on future CFL studies (§6). 2. Background Non-IIDness. Data heterogeneity implies non-identically distributed data among FL clients [23], [24]. To capture such heterogeneity, we consider the FL system that has N clients, each of which has a local training dataset di, where i = 1 , . . . , N. We denote D = SN i=1 di the joint training dataset. We consider there is k different data distributions, D1, · · · , Dk, and that N clients participate into k disjoint clusters, S1, . . . ,Sk. We consider that for each client i ∈ S j, di contains IID data drawn from Dj, where j ∈ [k]. Specifically, we formalize new cluster poisoning attacks (§4.2) and the exploitation of client-drift effect in CFL schemes (§4.3). • We introduce Cluster-U-M and Cluster-U-D attacks, and analyse them with CFL schemes (§4.4). • We extensively evaluate the attacks in practical FL settings, considering compromised proportions and client scales, even when state-of-the-art defenses FLTrust [10] and FLAME [33] are employed (§5). • We discuss new defense solutions with experimental evaluation and shed light on future CFL studies (§6). 2. The presence of non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data among clients poses a critical challenge to the deployment of Federated Learning (FL) in practice. In response, state-of-the-art solutions known as Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) schemes, such as FL+HC and PACFL, have emerged to tackle this issue. Their main innovation is to cluster non-IID clients into groups of IID clients, such that techniques designated for IID scenarios can be easily applicable. Nonetheless, the robustness of CFL schemes remains largely unexplored, and existing Byzantinerobust defence mechanisms prove inadequate in CFL schemes and non-IID data settings. In this work, we present novel powerful CFL-specific poisoning attacks, named Cluster-U-M and Cluster-U-D. These attacks are designed to significantly reduce the model utility, measured in terms of test accuracy, for benign clients participating in the CFL schemes. Notably, these attacks remain agnostic, requiring no adversarial knowledge regarding defense solutions and benign clients themselves. At a high level, the attacks involve two steps, including cluster poisoning attacks and client-drift exploitation within clusters. The former induces the grouping of clients with different training distributions, and the latter amplifies the difference between each client's optimum and their group's average aggregation. We extensively evaluate the impact of these attacks using FL+HC and PACFL schemes on both small and large scales. The evaluation results demonstrate that the attacks can compromise up to 54% of clients, with a maximum accuracy loss of 48%. Even with only 0.1% clients compromised, which represents a minimal practical adversarial effort, these attacks can still victimize around 4% clients. We evaluate the effectiveness of two stateof-the-art Byzantine-robust defence mechanisms, i.e., FLTrust and FLAME, in countering Cluster-U-M and Cluster-U-D, and find that the attacks can victimize up to 38% of clients with an accuracy loss of 18-38% under the FL+HC scheme.
